Wayside
wā'sīd
n. (the edge of a road; the place of watching, of ambush, and in the parable the trodden ground where seed cannot enter)
From way and side. The Authorized Version prints it as one word in 1 Samuel and the Psalms, and as two — way side — in the parable of the sower; the ground is the same, the hard-packed edge of a path.

Biblical Definition

The wayside is where a man sits to watch for news he dreads. “And when he came, lo, Eli sat upon a seat by the wayside watching: for his heart trembled for the ark of God” (1 Samuel 4:13). It is also where enemies work: “The proud have hid a snare for me, and cords; they have spread a net by the wayside; they have set gins for me” (Psalm 140:5). The most familiar use is the first soil of the parable: “And when he sowed, some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up” (Matthew 13:4). The Lord interprets it Himself, and the interpretation turns on the ground's hardness: “When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. This is he which received seed by the way side” (Matthew 13:19). The path is not barren for lack of seed or sun; it is barren because it has been walked on until nothing can get in. The seed lies exposed on the surface, and the birds take what never went down. Wayside ground is made, not born — every foot that crosses a field packs it a little harder.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines way-side as the side of the way, the border of a road, and way as a passage, road or street.

expand to see more

WAY-SIDE, n. The side of the way; the border of a road.

WAY, n. Literally, a passing; hence, a passage; the place of passing; a road; a highway; a street.

SNARE, n. An instrument for catching animals, particularly birds, by the leg.

2. Any thing by which one is entangled and brought into trouble.

GIN, n. A trap; a snare.

Key Scripture

Matthew 13:4 — "And when he sowed, some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them up:"

Matthew 13:19 — "When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. This is he which received seed by the way side."

1 Samuel 4:13 — "And when he came, lo, Eli sat upon a seat by the wayside watching: for his heart trembled for the ark of God. And when the man came into the city, and told it, all the city cried out."

Psalm 140:5 — "The proud have hid a snare for me, and cords; they have spread a net by the wayside; they have set gins for me. Selah."

Modern Corruption

Wayside hearing is treated as a fixed type of person rather than a condition of ground that traffic produced and grace can break up.

expand to see more

The four soils are often preached as four kinds of people, sorted permanently, so that the wayside hearer is simply a reprobate and the matter ends there. The figure itself resists that. A path is hard because it has been walked on; it was field once. Jeremiah and Hosea both command what follows from this — break up your fallow ground — and the ploughman's answer to a beaten track is not to declare it a different substance but to break it open. The doctrine of election is not touched by saying so; God is the one who gives the new heart, and the means He uses include the plough of the law and the preaching that turns the surface over.

The second and more searching application is that hardness is produced by traffic, and traffic is the ordinary condition of a modern life. The wayside hearer in Matthew 13:19 is not hostile; he simply understandeth it not, and the wicked one takes the seed before it can sink. That is an exact portrait of hearing a sermon while the mind is already elsewhere. Eli sat by the wayside because his heart trembled for the ark of God, and even his watching was too late to change what he had failed to correct in his sons. A church that fills every hour and leaves no ground unwalked should not be surprised when the seed lies on the surface.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hodos (G3598), a way or road — Matthew 13:4, 13:19; Hebrew derek and yad derek, the hand or side of the way — 1 Samuel 4:13, Psalm 140:5.

expand to see more

Greek para ten hodon — beside the way; Matthew 13:4, Mark 4:4, Luke 8:5, the first of the four soils.

Greek harpazo (G726) — to snatch away by force; Matthew 13:19, of the wicked one taking the seed.

Hebrew derek — a way, road, journey; the common word behind the Old Testament uses.

Hebrew moqesh — a snare, a gin; Psalm 140:5, set by the wayside where men must pass.

Hosea 10:12 supplies the answer to hard ground: break up your fallow ground, for it is time to seek the LORD.

Usage

"“Some seeds fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured them” — nothing went down."

"“Eli sat upon a seat by the wayside watching” — the place of dreaded news."

"A path is hard because it was walked on; it was field once."
